lessonLine: Grade 10 · Algebra II · Topic 3: Polynomial Functions · Lesson 3-3 — Identities with Polynomials
objectives: Apply polynomial identities for multiplication, factoring, and simplification.
Expand a power of a binomial by applying the binomial theorem.
vocabList: Binomial Coefficient ; binomial theorem ; Identity ; Pascal’s triangle

outcome: Students will understand and prove a polynomial identity by expanding one side until it matches the other (objective 1; HSA.APR.C.4).
Students will apply $(a+b)^{2}$, $(a-b)^{2}$ and $(a+b)(a-b)$ to expand, factor and simplify, and use them to calculate numbers quickly (objective 2; HSA.SSE.A.2).
Students will expand a power of a binomial using Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem (objective 3; (+)HSA.APR.C.5).
Students will use identities to describe numerical relationships, such as $99\times101=100^{2}-1$ and Pythagorean triples (HSA.APR.C.4).
Three teaching days this week. If time runs short, cut Smart Production — never the Mastery Gate.
preclass: Pre-session home journey (already issued, with Lesson 3-4): watch “How to Use the Binomial Theorem”, study two worked examples, answer three ungraded readiness questions. Submitted on the LMS before class.
Readiness questions: expand $(x+1)^{4}$ from row 4 of Pascal's triangle; evaluate $101^{2}-99^{2}$ with an identity; expand $(x-2)^{3}$.
Evidence: the LMS answers feed the Diagnose.
diagTool: 3-question Quizizz (≤ 4 minutes) — the slide-4 checks: expand $(x+4)(x-4)$; simplify $(3x)^{2}$; evaluate $(a+b)^{2}$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}$ for $a=3$, $b=2$.
diagGap: Expected gaps — Q2: $(3x)^{2}$ written as $3x^{2}$. Q3: the two values are treated as equal, which is the whole point of the lesson.
Routing: 0–1 correct → re-teach expanding two brackets and squaring a product.  2 → straight to the three square patterns.  3 → begin Investigate early.
instruction: Slide 5 — Proving an identity (objective 1; HSA.APR.C.4). $(x+3)^{2}=x^{2}+6x+9$ is proved by expanding one side; $(x+2)^{2}=x^{2}+4$ is disproved by one value, $x=1$: $9\ne5$.
Slide 6 — Identities for multiplication and factoring (objective 2; HSA.SSE.A.2). $(2x-5)^{2}=4x^{2}-20x+25$; $9x^{2}-49=(3x-7)(3x+7)$; $x^{3}-27=(x-3)(x^{2}+3x+9)$.
Slide 7 — Identities and numbers (HSA.APR.C.4). $48^{2}=(50-2)^{2}=2304$; $99\times101=100^{2}-1=9999$; $x=3$, $y=2$ gives the triple $5,\ 12,\ 13$.

Slide 8 — Binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle (objective 3; (+)HSA.APR.C.5). $(x+2)^{4}=x^{4}+8x^{3}+24x^{2}+32x+16$; $(2x-1)^{3}=8x^{3}-12x^{2}+6x-1$; the $x^{2}$ coefficient of $(x+3)^{5}$ is $270$.
Narration focus — never lose the middle term; the powers of the first term fall while the powers of the second rise.
quickCheck: Expected: $4x^{2}+12x+9$. Watch for $4x^{2}+9$ (middle term lost) and $2x^{2}+12x+9$ (only $x$ squared).
guided: Two identical “Give it a go” problems, worked with the teacher:
(1) Expand $(x+5)^{2}$ and factor $x^{2}-64$.  (2) Use row 3 of Pascal's triangle to expand $(x+1)^{3}$.
Worked live; students self-mark and circle their OWN first error.
independent: “Choose Your Route” sheet with live Pear Deck feedback. Routes name the task, not the student.

PRACTICE — Secure the method. Six cards: expand, factor and use a row of Pascal's triangle; then find the error in a squared bracket and prove one identity. Done when: the middle term $2ab$ is written, its sign follows the bracket, and each answer is checked with a number.
APPLY — Use it in context. A solar-panel field, an event hall, a divisibility proof and $(x-2)^{5}$. Done when: the identity used is named and each answer says what it means.
INVESTIGATE — Find out why. Prove $(a+b)^{2}-(a-b)^{2}=4ab$, build a Pythagorean triple, and explain the row sums $2^{n}$. Done when: the argument starts from a known identity or a full expansion.
Page 3: compare three expansion routes, judge three claims, test a What if...? idea. Every student sits the same Mastery Gate.
production: Non-routine transfer task — this context has not appeared in practice (slide 11).
A model square plaza in the Wadi Hanifa restoration has side $x$ m. A uniform paved walkway $3$ m wide runs all round the outside. The model values are invented for practice.

(a) Write the side and area of the plaza with its walkway and expand. (b) Write the walkway area as a difference of squares and factor it. (c) For $x=24$ find the walkway area from the factored form and check it directly.
Students then hand their reasoning to the AI challenger.
criteria: Minimum standard: the identity named, every step shown, the factored form used for the number, units (m, m$^{2}$).
Role of AI: challenger only — “Challenge my reasoning and point out any step I have not justified.” Never “solve this”.
Completed independently: the written justification for (a)–(c).
evidence: “Time to Check” — one individual task. No notes, no partner, no AI.
1. Expand $(4x-3)^{2}$.  2. Factor $49x^{2}-81$.  3. Expand $(x+1)^{5}$ with Pascal's triangle.
Done when: question 1 keeps the middle term and question 3 uses row 5.
Scored live in Pear Deck and logged in the Impact Dashboard.
refinement: Students revise their plaza reasoning using the AI challenger’s feedback and the teacher’s micro-conference note.

Final product (Canva one-pager, photographed solution, or 45-second voice note): the identity named, the proof, ONE non-example ($(a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}$ disproved by a number), and why the walkway area factors as $12(x+3)$.
differentiation: PRACTICE — Secure the method. Six cards, a find-the-error line and a proof box. Done when: the middle term is written and each answer is checked with a number.
APPLY — Use it in context. A solar field, a seating count, a divisibility proof and a fifth power. Done when: the identity is named.
INVESTIGATE — Find out why. A proof, a Pythagorean triple and the row sums. Done when: the argument starts from a known identity.
No student is labelled; every student sits the same Mastery Gate.
saudi: Wadi Hanifa plaza, a solar-panel field and an event hall; invented values.
exams: SAT — Advanced Math: if $a-b=3$ and $ab=10$, then $a^{2}+b^{2}=29$. Trap: answering $9+10=19$.
GAT (Qudurat) — $49\times51$ versus $2500$: $49\times51=2499$, so $2500$ is greater. Trap: assuming they are equal.
SAAT (Tahsili) — the coefficient of $x$ in $(x+3)^{4}$ is $108$. Trap: using $4\times3=12$.
adaptive: Entry branch — the Quizizz result routes each student to the re-teach table, straight to the new content, or the Investigate prompt.
Mid-lesson branch — Pear Deck flags error patterns during independent practice; flagged students get a 2-minute micro-conference while others continue.
Exit branch — the Mastery Gate routes each student: PASS → Enrichment & Challenge; NOT YET → Targeted Learning Clinic at the start of the next lesson.
Routing is communicated privately through the LMS, never read aloud.
publication: Published to the class LMS portfolio; the strongest go on the Mathematics Department wall.

plan2026.tools: Quizizz (diagnostic) · Pear Deck (live practice feedback) · Whiteboards · Desmos (checking an identity with two graphs) · Canva (final product) · Squared paper
plan2026.resources: Lesson presentation (15 slides) · “Choose Your Route” activity (3 pages) · Wayground kick-off
competencies: Proving a polynomial identity and disproving a false one with a number.
Expanding $(a\pm b)^{n}$ with Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem.
technology: Quizizz live diagnostic with instant gap analysis.
Desmos: graph both sides of an identity and see one curve.
reallife: A plaza and its walkway: the area is a difference of squares.
values: Accuracy — the middle term and its sign are written down before they are used.
soft: Explaining in words why $(a+b)^{2}$ is not $a^{2}+b^{2}$.
hard: Proving an identity by expanding one side.
Expanding a binomial power with Pascal's triangle.
phases: FIKR Phase 1 — Diagnose. 3-question Quizizz: difference of squares, squaring a product, comparing $(a+b)^{2}$ with $a^{2}+b^{2}$. Results read as a gap map and used to route students.
FIKR Phase 2 — Targeted Instruction. Proving an identity; the square and difference patterns; identities and numbers; Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem.
FIKR Phase 3 — Practice. Two identical “Give it a go” problems; then students choose a route and may switch. Compare routes and judge the claim. Pear Deck feedback.
FIKR Phase 4 — Production. Wadi Hanifa plaza and walkway; AI as challenger only.
FIKR Phase 5 — Proof of Learning. “Time to Check”. No notes, no partner, no AI.
FIKR Phase 6 — Smart Production. Make a model identity, prove it, swap and test; publish to the LMS portfolio.
assessment: Diagnostic quiz — gap map, not a grade.
Whiteboard check (80% threshold) and “Give it a go” — self-marked.
Project task sheet against its “Done when…” criteria.
“Time to Check” — Mastery Gate, scored live.
Final product graded on reasoning and clarity.
plan2026.closure: Two minutes of peer show-and-tell, then: “Which is harder — remembering the middle term, or choosing which identity to use?”
plan2026.homework: Upload the final product to the LMS portfolio. Pear Deck practice set (12 questions, choose your route). Schoology homework quiz for Lesson 3-3. Watch the flipped video for Lesson 3-4. Clinic group: bring your Time to Check paper.

classwork.subtitle: Show all your working. Read the vertex with the signs flipped, divide 4p by 4, and measure to the focus and the directrix. A correct answer with no working is only half an answer.

sections.h: Part A — Focus, directrix and the equation
text: 1.  A parabola has focus $(0,2)$ and directrix $y=-2$. For the point $P(4,2)$, find $PF$ and $PD$. Is $P$ on the parabola? Then derive the equation using $PF=PD$.
2.  Derive the equation of the parabola with focus $(0,5)$ and directrix $y=-5$. State $p$.
3.  Write the equation of the parabola with focus $(0,-4)$ and directrix $y=4$. Which way does it open?

sections.h: Part B — Reading the equation and the graph
text: 4.  Find the vertex, $p$, the focus, the directrix and the axis of symmetry.
5.  Find the vertex, $p$, the focus and the directrix. Which way does it open?
6.  The graph shows a parabola. Its vertex and focus are marked. Read them, then write the equation in standard form and the directrix.

sections.h: Part C — Graphing from key features
text: 7.  Graph $(x-1)^{2}=8\,(y+1)$ on the grid. Mark the vertex, the focus and the directrix, and the two points at the height of the focus.
8.  Graph $y^{2}=-8x$ on the grid. Mark the vertex, the focus and the directrix, and the two points at the height of the focus.
9.  Complete the square and find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.
10.  Complete the square and find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.
11.  Divide first, then complete the square. Find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.

sections.h: Part E — In context and in your own words
text: 12.  A model fountain jet on the Jeddah waterfront has its apex at $(0,8)$ and lands at $(\pm12,\,0)$ (metres, model values). Write its equation and find the focus. How high is the jet at $x=6$?
13.  A model satellite dish is $1.8$ m wide and $0.27$ m deep. Put the vertex at the origin, find $4p$ and say how far the receiver sits from the vertex.
14.  Show that the width of $x^{2}=4py$ at the height of the focus is $4\lvert p\rvert$. Use it to find the two points of $x^{2}=20y$ at that height.

pbl.title: Jeddah Satellite Dish Installer
pbl.subtitle: A 20-minute group project. Work in fours. Every member signs the sheet.
pbl.driving: A Jeddah installer has four dishes and one receiver arm that is 1.1 m long. Which dishes can hold the receiver exactly at the focus, and what does the shape of the dish tell you?
situation: A classroom model (invented for practice, not real figures): each dish is a parabola with its vertex at the origin, opening upward. Its width and depth are in the table. The receiver must sit at the focus, a distance $p$ above the vertex.

For each dish the group finds $4p$ from the rim point, writes the equation, finds $p$, and says whether a $1.1$ m arm is long enough. Then the group explains how the depth of a dish changes its focal length.
steps: For each dish, write the rim point $(x_{1},y_{1})$: half the width across, the full depth up. Write $x^{2}=4py$ with the rim point substituted.
Find $4p$ and $p$ for every dish and write each equation. Fill the table.
Which dishes can hold the receiver at the focus with a $1.1$ m arm? Check one dish: the rim point is equally far from the focus and the directrix.
What happens to $p$ as the dishes get deeper for their width? Which dish is the most tightly curved?
One sentence for the installer: how can you tell where the receiver goes from the width and depth alone?

standards: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it.
Prove polynomial identities and use them to describe numerical relationships.

Know and apply the Binomial Theorem for the expansion of (x + y)n in powers of x and y for a positive integer n, where x and y are any numbers, with coefficients determined for example by Pascal's Triangle.
